title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: Before the course of taking the waters was over, Prince Shtcherbatsky — who had gone on from Carlsbad to Baden and Kissingen to look up Russian friends, to get a breath of Russian air, as he put it — came back to his wife and daughter.

The prince and princess took completely opposite views of life abroad. The princess thought everything was charming, and despite her settled standing in Russian society she tried, abroad, to play the European fashionable lady — which she wasn't, for the simple reason that she was a thoroughly Russian gentlewoman; so she came across as affected, which didn't quite suit her. The prince, on the contrary, found everything foreign loathsome, was sick of European life, clung to his Russian habits, and went out of his way to seem less European abroad than he really was.

The prince came back thinner, the skin hanging in loose pouches on his cheeks, but in the highest of spirits. His good humor grew even greater when he saw Kitty completely recovered. The news of Kitty's friendship with Madame Stahl and Varenka, and what the princess told him about some change she had noticed in Kitty, troubled him and stirred up his habitual jealousy of anything that drew his daughter away from him, his old fear that she might have slipped out of his reach into regions he could not enter. But these unpleasant feelings were drowned, as always, in the sea of kindness and good humor that was always in him — and more so than ever after his Carlsbad cure.

The day after his arrival, the prince — in his long overcoat, with his Russian wrinkles and baggy cheeks propped up by a starched collar — set off with his daughter to the springs in the brightest possible mood.

It was a lovely morning: the bright, cheerful houses with their little gardens, the sight of the red-faced, red-armed, beer-drinking German waitresses working away merrily, did the heart good. But the closer they got to the springs, the more often they passed sick people, and these looked more pitiable than ever against the everyday prosperity of German life. Kitty no longer felt the contrast. The bright sun, the dazzling green of the foliage, the strains of music were for her the natural setting of all these familiar faces, whose deepening emaciation or signs of recovery she had been watching. But to the prince the brightness and gaiety of the June morning, and the sound of the orchestra playing a fashionable waltz, and above all the look of the healthy attendants, seemed obscene and monstrous when set beside these slowly shuffling, dying figures gathered together from all over Europe. With his favorite daughter on his arm, and even with the feeling of pride and almost of recovered youth that came with it, he felt awkward — almost ashamed — of his brisk step and his sturdy, stout limbs. He felt almost like a man who had forgotten his clothes in a crowd.

"Introduce me to your new friends," he said to his daughter, pressing her hand with his elbow. "I even like your horrid Soden for making you well again. Only it's gloomy here, very gloomy. Who's that?"

Kitty named all the people they met, some of whom she knew and some not. At the garden entrance they ran into the blind lady, Madame Berthe, with her guide, and the prince was delighted to see the old Frenchwoman's face light up at the sound of Kitty's voice. She at once started talking to him with French exaggerated politeness, congratulating him on having such a charming daughter, praising Kitty to the skies right in front of her, calling her a treasure, a pearl, a consoling angel.
"Well, then she's the second angel," the prince said, smiling. "She calls Mademoiselle Varenka angel number one."
"Oh! Mademoiselle Varenka, she really is an angel, allez," Madame Berthe agreed.
In the arcade they met Varenka herself. She was walking briskly toward them, carrying an elegant red bag.
"Here's papa, come at last," Kitty said to her.

Varenka made — simply and naturally, as she did everything — a gesture somewhere between a bow and a curtsey, and at once began speaking to the prince without shyness, naturally, the way she spoke to everyone.
"Of course I know you; I know you very well," the prince said to her with a smile, in which Kitty was glad to detect that her father liked her friend. "Where are you off to in such a hurry?"
"Maman is here," she said, turning to Kitty. "She hasn't slept all night, and the doctor told her to go outside. I'm taking her her work."
"So that's angel number one?" said the prince, when Varenka had gone on.
Kitty could see that her father had meant to make fun of Varenka but couldn't, because he liked her.
"Come on, then, we'll see all your friends," he went on, "even Madame Stahl, if she's willing to recognize me."
"Why, did you know her, papa?" Kitty asked anxiously, catching the glint of irony that lit up in the prince's eyes at the name of Madame Stahl.
"I used to know her husband, and her a little too, before she went over to the Pietists."
"What's a Pietist, papa?" Kitty asked, dismayed to discover that what she so prized in Madame Stahl had a name attached to it.
"I don't quite know myself. I only know that she thanks God for everything, for every misfortune, and even thanks God that her husband died. Which is rather funny, since they didn't get on at all."

"Who's that? What a piteous face!" he asked, spotting a sick man of medium height sitting on a bench, wearing a brown overcoat and white trousers that hung in odd folds about his long, fleshless legs. The man lifted his straw hat to show his scanty curly hair and a high forehead that was painfully red from the press of the hat.

"That's Petrov, an artist," Kitty answered, blushing. "And that's his wife," she added, pointing to Anna Pavlovna, who, as though on cue, at the very moment they came near, moved off after a child that had run down a path.
"Poor man! And what a nice face he has!" said the prince. "Why don't you go up to him? He wanted to speak to you."
"Well, then let's go," said Kitty, turning around resolutely. "How are you feeling today?" she asked Petrov.
Petrov got up, leaning on his stick, and looked shyly at the prince.
"This is my daughter," the prince said. "Allow me to introduce myself."
The painter bowed and smiled, showing his strangely dazzling white teeth.
"We were expecting you yesterday, princess," he said to Kitty. He staggered as he said it, then repeated the movement on purpose, trying to pass it off as deliberate.
"I meant to come, but Varenka said Anna Pavlovna had sent word that you weren't going."
"Not going!" said Petrov, blushing and at once starting to cough, his eyes searching for his wife. "Anita! Anita!" he called loudly, and the swollen veins stood out like cords on his thin white neck.
Anna Pavlovna came over.
"So you sent word to the princess that we weren't going!" he whispered to her angrily, his voice giving out.
"Good morning, princess," said Anna Pavlovna, with a forced smile utterly unlike her former manner. "Very pleased to meet you," she said to the prince. "You've been long expected, prince."

"What did you send word to the princess that we weren't going for?" the artist whispered hoarsely again, even more angrily, plainly furious that his voice failed him and he couldn't put into his words the force he wanted.
"Oh, mercy on us! I thought we weren't going," his wife answered crossly.
"What, when —" He coughed and waved his hand. The prince raised his hat and moved off with his daughter.
"Ah, ah!" he sighed deeply. "Oh, poor things!"

"Yes, papa," Kitty answered. "And you should know they have three children, no servant, and almost no income. He gets something from the Academy," she went on quickly, trying to drown out the distress that Anna Pavlovna's strange change of manner had stirred in her.

"Oh, here's Madame Stahl," said Kitty, pointing to an invalid carriage, in which, propped on pillows, something in gray and blue was lying under a sunshade. This was Madame Stahl. Behind her stood the gloomy, healthy-looking German workman who pushed the carriage. Close by stood a flaxen-haired Swedish count whom Kitty knew by name. Several invalids were lingering near the low carriage, staring at the lady as if she were a curiosity.

The prince walked up to her, and Kitty caught again that disconcerting glint of irony in his eyes. He went up to Madame Stahl and addressed her with extreme courtesy and warmth, in that excellent French so few people speak nowadays.
"I don't know if you remember me, but I must remind you of myself, so that I can thank you for your kindness to my daughter," he said, lifting his hat and not putting it on again.
"Prince Alexander Shtcherbatsky," said Madame Stahl, raising onto him her heavenly eyes, in which Kitty caught a hint of annoyance. "Delighted! I have grown very fond of your daughter."
"You are still in poor health?"
"Yes; I'm used to it," said Madame Stahl, and she introduced the prince to the Swedish count.
"You've hardly changed at all," the prince said to her. "It's been ten or eleven years since I had the honor of seeing you."

"Yes; God sends the cross and sends the strength to bear it. Sometimes one wonders what the point of this life can be? — The other side!" she said sharply to Varenka, who had rearranged the rug over her feet in a way she didn't like.
"To do good, presumably," said the prince with a twinkle in his eye.

"That isn't for us to judge," Madame Stahl said, catching the shade of expression on the prince's face. "So you'll send me that book, dear count? I'm very grateful to you," she said to the young Swede.
"Ah!" cried the prince, catching sight of the Moscow colonel standing nearby, and with a bow to Madame Stahl he moved off with his daughter and the Moscow colonel, who joined them.
"There's our aristocracy for you, prince!" the Moscow colonel said with pointed irony. He nursed a grudge against Madame Stahl for not making his acquaintance.
"She's just the same," the prince replied.
"Did you know her before her illness, prince — that is, before she took to her bed?"
"Yes. She took to her bed right in front of me," said the prince.
"They say it's been ten years since she stood on her feet."
"She doesn't stand up because her legs are too short. She has a very bad figure."
"Papa, that can't be!" cried Kitty.
"That's what wicked tongues say, my dear. And your Varenka catches it too," he added. "Oh, these invalid ladies!"
"Oh, no, papa!" Kitty protested warmly. "Varenka worships her. And she does so much good! Ask anyone! Everyone knows her and Aline Stahl."
"Perhaps," said the prince, squeezing her hand with his elbow; "but it's better when one does good in a way that you can ask everyone and no one knows."

Kitty did not reply, not because she had nothing to say, but because she had no wish to share even with her father what she was really thinking. But, strange to say, although she had so resolved not to let her father's view influence her, not to let him into her inner sanctuary, she felt that the heavenly image of Madame Stahl, which she had carried in her heart for a whole month, had vanished and would not come back — the way a fantastic figure made of clothes thrown down at random vanishes the instant you see it is just a garment lying there. What was left was a woman with short legs, who lay down because her figure was bad, and who badgered patient Varenka about the rug. And no effort of imagination could bring the former Madame Stahl back to Kitty.
